title: Charles Wesley's hymns
hookLine: John's brother writes hymns like O for a thousand tongues and Love divine, all loves excelling

cards: John Wesley rode the roads. His younger brother Charles rode them too, and did something else on the way: he wrote hymns. Lots of them.
Tradition says he composed lines on horseback and, when one came, would stop at a house and ask for pen and ink before he lost it.
If you've sung Hark! the herald angels sing in a church at Christmas, you've sung Charles Wesley. If you've been at a wedding where they sang Love divine, all loves excelling, you've sung him too.
Both brothers preached, and Charles also set the message to music.

teach.b: Here are the lines that open the hymn as it's usually sung today: "O for a thousand tongues to sing My great Redeemer's praise, The glories of my God and King, The triumphs of his grace!"
The idea is simple and a little funny. One tongue isn't enough. Charles wants a thousand, because he can't say it all with one.

Some readers hear in it the spirit of the Methodist revival: gratitude too big for a single voice. His hymns did a quiet job too. A hymn sung every week is carried in memory, whether or not the singer can read.

People learned what the revival believed, about grace, about the cross, about a heart made new, by singing it until it was theirs. Another: "Love divine, all loves excelling, Joy of heaven, to earth come down."
Love, here, is a name for God, and it comes down to earth; the hymn goes on to ask that love to make its home in the singer.

His hymns fit an instruction in the letter to the Ephesians, where Christians are told to be filled with the Spirit, "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."
Speaking to yourselves: a hymn isn't only sung up to God.

It's sung across the room, to each other, and back into your own chest. And the last psalm has a line that fits too: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." A thousand tongues, every breath.
Today his hymns are sung in churches of many kinds, far beyond the Methodists.

how: Charles Wesley's hymns appear in the hymnbooks of different churches, and congregations sing them on Sundays and at Christmas, weddings and funerals, often standing together.

practice: Say or sing today's first lines: O for a thousand tongues to sing my great Redeemer's praise. Then, since one tongue isn't enough, let the things you're grateful for come up one at a time, each with its own voice.
If you pray, let that list be your praise; if you don't, let it grow.
